text:
Montreal has not lost in regulation in eleven games (8-0-3), and the run has the feel of a team that keeps finding a way. The chances have been split right down the middle in that stretch, 50% of the expected goals, which is the quality of the shots each side gets. What has tipped close games is Jacob Fowler. The young goalie is at .925 with 12.1 goals saved above expected this season, and 6.1 of those came in his last five starts. Tuesday's 2-1 overtime loss to Minnesota, on what The Hockey News called Carey Price's big night at the Bell Centre, was the rare one where the other goalie, Jesper Wallstedt, stole the show.

Boston has won four straight, outscoring teams 18-9, and here is the uncomfortable part for Bruins fans: the chances only half back it. Their goal difference is +26 on +1.4 expected. Finishing (9.1 goals above what their chances usually produce) and goaltending (15.5 goals saved above expected, 10.2 of them Jeremy Swayman's) are carrying the load. Swayman made 40 saves against Florida on Sunday. That works until it doesn't, and the Bruins come in after three days off.

Both teams are missing a young forward. Ivan Demidov (ankle) is on injured reserve, and Cole Caufield has slid into his spot beside Juraj Slafkovský and Alex Newhook, with Zachary Bolduc moving onto the top power play. Caufield has points in four straight and 30 headlines in two weeks about a 50-goal pace. Boston is without James Hagens (back), who has 12 points in 17 games; Marat Khusnutdinov took his place next to Elias Lindholm and Casey Mittelstadt.

Mittelstadt is our Sleeper: a third-liner with 2.5 expected goals in his last ten, against a Montreal side that allows the sixth-most expected goals per 60. We give him a 21% chance to score. Montreal also takes 5.2 penalties a game, which is a lot of time to give David Pastrnak and Pavel Zacha, both on four-game point streaks. Our numbers have the Bruins at 3.21 expected goals to Montreal's 2.94.
headline: Two hot goalies, one old rivalry
